content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a prevalent inherited condition worldwide, characterized by chronic health complications and reduced life expectancy. Hydroxyurea, also known as hydroxycarbamide, is an oral chemotherapeutic agent that alleviates some clinical manifestations of SCD, particularly pain, by increasing levels of fetal hemoglobin (HbF). This review aimed to evaluate the effects of hydroxyurea on acute events such as pain crises, organ dysfunction, mortality, quality of life, and adverse effects. Additionally, it sought to determine whether the response to hydroxyurea varies based on SCD genotype, age, treatment duration, dosage, or healthcare setting. The review included nine randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,104 participants with SCD (HbSS, HbSC, or HbSβºthal genotypes). The studies ranged in duration from six to 30 months. The quality of evidence was assessed as moderate to low for most comparisons, with some outcomes, such as quality of life, mortality, and adverse events, being limited and imprecise. The findings primarily apply to individuals with HbSS and HbSβºthal genotypes, as evidence for other genotypes and age groups was insufficient. Hydroxyurea versus placebo: Five studies, including 784 adults and children with HbSS or HbSβºthal genotypes, compared hydroxyurea to placebo. Four studies focused on individuals with severe disease, while one included participants with varying disease severities. Hydroxyurea likely reduces pain crises (measured by frequency, duration, intensity, hospitalizations, and opioid use) and life-threatening complications. However, no significant differences in mortality rates were observed, with 10 deaths reported across the studies but no treatment group differences (moderate-quality evidence). Hydroxyurea may improve HbF levels (low-quality evidence) and likely reduces neutrophil counts (moderate-quality evidence). There were no consistent differences in quality of life or adverse events, including serious or life-threatening events (low-quality evidence). Fewer cases of acute chest syndrome and blood transfusions were reported in the hydroxyurea groups. Hydroxyurea and phlebotomy versus transfusion and chelation: Two studies, involving 254 children with HbSS or HbSβºthal genotypes at risk of primary or secondary stroke, compared hydroxyurea with phlebotomy to transfusion with chelation. No consistent differences were observed in pain crises, mortality, adverse events (low-quality evidence), or life-threatening complications (moderate-quality evidence). Hydroxyurea with phlebotomy likely increased HbF levels and reduced neutrophil counts (moderate-quality evidence), but there were more cases of acute chest syndrome and infections. Quality of life was not reported. In the primary prevention study, no strokes occurred in either group. However, in the secondary prevention study, seven strokes occurred in the hydroxyurea and phlebotomy group, while none were reported in the transfusion and chelation group, leading to early termination of the study. Hydroxyurea versus observation: One study, involving 22 children with HbSS or HbSβºthal genotypes at risk of stroke, compared hydroxyurea to observation. Pain crises and quality of life were not reported. No differences were observed in life-threatening complications, mortality (no deaths in either group), or adverse events (very low-quality evidence). It remains uncertain whether hydroxyurea improves HbF levels or reduces neutrophil counts (very low-quality evidence). Treatment regimens with and without hydroxyurea: One study, involving 44 adults and children with HbSC genotype, compared treatment regimens with and without hydroxyurea. Pain crises, life-threatening complications, and quality of life were not reported. No differences were observed in mortality (no deaths in either group), adverse events, or neutrophil counts (very low-quality evidence). It is uncertain whether hydroxyurea improves HbF levels (very low-quality evidence). Conclusions: Hydroxyurea appears to reduce the frequency of pain episodes and other acute complications in individuals with HbSS or HbSβºthal genotypes and may prevent life-threatening neurological events in those at risk of primary stroke by maintaining transcranial Doppler velocities. However, evidence regarding its long-term benefits, particularly in preventing chronic complications of SCD, remains insufficient. There is also limited evidence to recommend a standard dose or dose-escalation strategy. The long-term risks of hydroxyurea, including its effects on fertility and reproduction, are not well understood. Additionally, there is a lack of evidence on its efficacy in individuals with the HbSC genotype. Future research should address these uncertainties to provide more comprehensive guidance on the use of hydroxyurea in SCD management.
